lines: Guerrilla warfare is how the weak fight the strong.
Small, mobile bands avoid big battles, strike where the enemy is weak, and vanish before it can hit back.
Let's break down how it works.
Picture a powerful army: tanks, trucks, and soldiers by the thousand.
Now picture the other side: a handful of fighters with rifles.
In an open battle, the small side gets crushed.
So guerrillas simply refuse to fight that battle.
Rule one: hit and run.
The guerrillas choose the time and the place. An ambush on a supply convoy. A raid on a lonely outpost.
They strike hard and fast, then disappear before reinforcements arrive.
Mao Zedong summed it up: the enemy advances, we retreat. The enemy camps, we harass. The enemy tires, we attack. The enemy retreats, we pursue.
Rule two: use the terrain.
Forests, mountains, swamps and cities let small groups hide from a much bigger force.
In Vietnam, fighters around Cu Chi dug a tunnel network more than two hundred kilometers long.
The enemy patrol arrives, and finds nobody.
Rule three: the people.
Mao wrote that a guerrilla must move among the people the way a fish swims in the sea.
Locals give food, shelter, new recruits, and most importantly, information: where the enemy is, and where it's going.
Lose the people's support, and the guerrilla has nowhere left to hide.
Rule four: hit the supply lines, not the strongest units.
An army can't fight without fuel, food and ammunition, and all of it moves on roads and railways.
In World War One, T. E. Lawrence and Arab fighters raided the Hejaz Railway again and again.
In World War Two, Soviet and Yugoslav partisans blew up rail lines behind German lines, and tied down whole divisions far from the front.
The same ideas still work today, with new tools.
In 2022, as Russian columns pushed toward Kyiv, small Ukrainian teams with anti-tank weapons and cheap drones ambushed vehicles strung out along the roads.
A few people, a drone, and a good hiding spot could stop a convoy cold.
This creates a nightmare for the stronger army.
It has to guard every road, every bridge and every town. The guerrillas only have to hit one of them.
Spread out, the army is weak everywhere. Bunched up, it hands the countryside to the guerrillas.
So how do guerrillas win? Usually not by destroying the enemy army.
They win by not losing: making the war so long and so costly that the enemy decides to go home.
As Henry Kissinger put it: the guerrilla wins if he does not lose. The conventional army loses if it does not win.
Hit and run. Use the terrain. Win over the people. Cut the supply lines. And outlast the enemy.
That's guerrilla warfare.
